aiExplanation: This function calculates the **minimum Hamming distance** (positions where two arrays differ) after making as many **allowed swaps** as possible. First, it builds a **graph of connected positions** by creating a map where each position tracks which positions it can swap with; then it uses **depth-first search** (via the `find` function) to identify all positions in the same **connected component**, storing the reachable positions for each index in the `dp` array. Finally, it iterates through each position: if `source[i]` doesn't match `target[i]`, it searches for another position `j` within the same connected component that contains the needed value (`source[j] === target[i]`), and if found, performs the swap; if no valid swap exists, it increments the **mismatch counter** (`res`). The function returns the count of positions that remain different after all optimal swaps are made.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: The code solves the **minimum Hamming distance** problem by using **graph connectivity** to determine which array positions can indirectly swap values. First, it builds a **graph of allowed swaps** using a map where each position lists all positions it can directly swap with. Then, it performs **depth-first search (DFS)** from each position to find all positions in the same **connected component** (all positions reachable through a chain of swaps), storing these in the `dp` array. Finally, for each position where `source[i]` doesn't match `target[i]`, it searches for another mismatched position `j` in the same connected component where `source[j]` equals the needed `target[i]` value, and if found, **swaps them**. The function returns the count of positions that still don't match after performing all beneficial swaps—the minimum possible Hamming distance.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This code calculates the **minimum Hamming distance** (number of positions that can't be matched) between two arrays when you're allowed to swap elements. It uses a **Union-Find data structure** to group indices that can be swapped together—either directly (via `allowedSwaps`) or transitively through other swaps. For each group of indices, it counts how many times each value appears in the `source` array at those positions. Then, going through each position in the `target` array, it checks whether the needed value exists within that position's group (using up one occurrence if found, or incrementing the Hamming distance if not). The result is the total count of positions where the target value **can't** be obtained through any allowed swaps, which represents the minimum mismatches you can achieve.
